text:
Lennie Ryer CA c. Potten

2014 QCCS 3349

JP2056

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

N°:

500-17-065609-110

DATE :

July 3, 2014

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:

THE HONOURABLE

MARIE-ANNE PAQUETTE
, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

LENNIE RYER C.A.

Plaintiff

Cross-Defendant

v.

STEPHEN R. POTTEN

Defendant

Cross-Claimant

and

S.R. POTTEN ENTERPRISES LTD

Mis en cause

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

The Defendant Mr. Stephen R. Potten is the
founder, sole shareholder and officer of the Defendant company, S.R. Potten
Enterprises Ltd (the
Company
).

Since 1978, the Company

sells
and distributes barbecues and related accessories across Canada.

[
2
]

In 2010, the Plaintiff, Mr. Lennie Ryer and
his business partner, Mr. Mitchell Greenspoon, entered into discussions
with Mr. Potten to acquire the Company.  A letter of intent (
Letter of Intent

or
LOI
)
[1]
was executed, with the view of completing the transaction.

[
3
]

However, the acquisition was never completed.

[
4
]

Mr. Ryer blames the turn of events on
Mr. Potten’s bad faith and unlawful repudiation of his obligations under
the Letter of intent. He thus seeks $3,686,517.84 from Mr. Potten and the
Company, to compensate for the various damages allegedly incurred as a result.

[
5
]

Mr. Potten and the Company reply that the
transaction did not materialize for just and valid reasons.  They deny all
allegations of liability.  Mr. Potten furthermore seeks $350,000 as moral
and punitive damages resulting from Mr. Ryer’s allegedly abusive action
and harassment during the course of the present litigation and business
dispute.

[
6
]

Mr. Ryer’s main action is dismissed, with
costs.

[
7
]

The failure to complete the transaction
certainly does not result from the Defendants’ lack of good faith.
Mr. Potten was eager and willing to sell the Company.  He cooperated with
the due diligence process and in the pre contract negotiations.  The parties
also reasonably attempted to solve the disagreement which they faced on the
ownership of the profits earned until the final closing of the transaction,
unfortunately to no avail.

[
8
]

Mr. Potten’s Cross-Claim is also dismissed, with
costs.

[
9
]

First, Mr. Ryer’s action against
Mr. Potten and the Company is not in itself ill founded to the point of
constituting an abuse of right.

[
10
]

Second, even though Mr. Ryer acted
inappropriately in repeatedly communicating with Mr. Ryer by email pending
the current litigation, there is insufficient proof that such form of
harassment and immature behaviour by Mr. Ryer resulted directly in
substantive damages to Mr. Potten.

1.

THE FACTS

[
11
]

In the Fall of 2007, after working for close to
30 years building up and operating the Company, Mr. Potten decides to sell
it, with a view to retiring.

[
12
]

He thus mandates Mr. Stanley Mazoff,
President of Mazoff Management Ltd, to identify potential buyers and to provide
all the necessary assistance towards the conclusion of an agreement to sell the
Company.
[2]

[
13
]

In June 2010, through Mr. Mazoff,
Mr. Greenspoon and Mr. Ryer are informed of this business
opportunity.  Mr. Greenspoon is a lawyer with strong mergers and
acquisitions and investment banking experience.  Mr. Ryer, one of his
acquaintances, is a CA, also with significant mergers and acquisitions
experience.

[
14
]

On August 20, 2010, Messrs Ryer and
Greenspoon have lunch with Mr. Mazoff.  He then gives an overview of the
Company in question (consumer product, hard goods, EBITDA
[3]
),
without identifying it.  He also advances the rough figures of the vendor’s
target purchase price ($12 million overall, with $9 million at closing) and
closing date (2010 calendar year).

[
15
]

Messrs Ryer and Greenspoon have another
meeting with Mr. Mazoff, at Mr. Ryer’s house.  The Company’s
profitability for the last 30 years, its low number of employees, the good
support received by the Company’s banker and the owner’s willingness to retire
deepen their interest in the acquisition.

[
16
]

A meeting with Mr. Potten follows.

[
17
]

On October 6, 2010, Messrs Mazoff, Ryer and
Greenspoon meet with Mr. Potten at the Company’s premises in Lachine.
Mr. Potten then gives a detailed overview of the operations.  He walks
them through the warehouse, gives a history of the BBQ business, of the
margins, of the clients and of the expectations for the year in progress.  The
meeting is very cordial and collegial.

[
18
]

The next day, October 7, 2010, the parties sign
a Mutual Nondisclosure Agreement (
NDA
),
[4]
to
allow for the safe disclosure of confidential information between them.

[
19
]

The communication of more sensitive information
follows.

[
20
]

On October 21, 2010, Mr. Potten arranges a
meeting with the TD Bank, the Company’s banker for the last 20 years.  Mr. Bruno
Ciolfi, the TD Bank representative, attends the meeting, in which
Messrs Potten, Mazoff, Ryer and Greenspoon take part.  Mr. Ciolfi then
explains the banking arrangements of the Company.

[
21
]

Again, the tone of the meeting is very
positive.  Messrs Ryer and Greenspoon leave with the impression that TD
Bank would have no problem with carrying over business with them.
Mr. Potten instructs Mr. Ciolfi to provide whatever information
Messrs Ryer and Greenspoon want.

[
22
]

On October 26, 2010, bearing the Company’s
business cycle in mind, Mr. Mazoff reiterates the importance of closing
the transaction before the calendar year-end in the following terms:

When are you planning to meet with
Steve [(Mr. Potten)]?

We need to aim for a deal by the
end of the year for many reasons as already discussed
. One additional compelling reason is that
if a deal happens once
the season is well underway or almost done, Steve is going to want to keep a
big share of the year profits
.
[5]

[Emphasis added]

[
23
]

The Company indeed operates in the seasonal
business of selling and distributing BBQ and BBQ accessories to retail
customers across Canada.  As a result, the first half of the calendar year
(January to June) is marked with a peak in its activities and cash flow.  No
one disputes this state of facts, of which all the interested parties were
fully aware at all relevant times.

[
24
]

On October 28, 2010, two days later,
Messrs Potten, Mazoff, Greenspoon and Ryer have a lunch meeting.
Communication of further information follows.

[
25
]

Various communications and exchanges also occur
between the potential buyers and Roynat Capital (
Roynat
), the lenders
whom they approached to finance the acquisition.
[6]

[
26
]

On December 17, 2010, Messrs Ryer and
Greenspoon secure an offer of financing from Roynat.
[7]

This offer to finance is contingent upon the completion of the due diligence
contemplated in the letter of intent to be signed.

[
27
]

On December 22, 2010, Messrs Ryer and
Potten sign the Letter of Intent.
[8]

[
28
]

The Letter of Intent authorizes the potential
buyers to conduct proper due diligence and contemplates a closing before
February 22, 2011.
[9]
The other relevant provisions of the Letter of Intent will be
further discussed later in the present judgment.

[
29
]

On January 12, 2010, the potential buyers
introduce Mr. Potten to Roynat.  This occurs at a meeting at the Company,
attended by Messrs Ryer, Greenspoon, Mazoff, Potten and Éric Krause,
representative of Roynat.

[
30
]

Once again, the tone of the meeting is very
positive. Mr. Potten eloquently describes the business, its cycle and the
competitive landscape.  Roynat is impressed with Mr. Potten’s detailed
knowledge of the business and remains interested in financing the transaction,
subject to satisfactory due diligence.  Mr. Potten undertakes to provide
as much information as he can.

[
31
]

Mr. Ryer arranges a further meeting with
Mr. Potten for February 17, 2011, with a view to completing the due
diligence within the delay stipulated in the Letter of Intent
(February 22, 2011).

[
32
]

In the morning of February 17, 2011,
Messrs Ryer and Greenspoon meet with TD Bank. Later in the day (4:02
p.m.), they agree on the terms of TD Bank’s continuing financial support, and
on the amount of the personal guarantees which the TD Bank requires from Messrs Ryer
and Greenspoon.
[10]

[
33
]

On February 17, 2011, few hours before the
scheduled time, Mr. Potten cancels the meeting.

[
34
]

The versions vary as to the reasons which were
then exposed to justify the cancellation. They will be discussed later in the
present judgment.

[
35
]

After this cancellation, Mr. Ryer
approaches Mr. Mazoff to request an extension of the Letter of Intent and
of the due diligence delay.
[11]

[
36
]

The parties never end up agreeing on such an
extension.

[
37
]

They face a major disagreement on the ownership
of the 2011 profits.

[
38
]

On March 8, 2011, another meeting is organized
at the initiative of Mr. Potten.  He then proposes revised deal terms,
which he deems properly account for the ownership of the 2011 profits.
[12]

[
39
]

Messrs Ryer and Greenspoon are extremely
dissatisfied with the proposed revised terms.

[
40
]

They walk away.

[
41
]

The parties were unable to overcome their
disagreement on the issue of the ownership of the profits earned up to the
closing date.  Both parties were adamant as to their respective positions.  The
clash turned out to be fatal for the deal.

2.

the position of the parties

2.1

Mr. Ryer

[
42
]

Mr. Ryer contends that after signing the Letter
of Intent, Mr. Potten experienced “seller’s remorse” and changed his mind.
He either lost interest or became prepared to proceed with the transaction, solely
on terms significantly different from those agreed to in the Letter of Intent.

[
43
]

To this end, he would have deliberately thwarted
Mr. Ryer’s attempt to carry out the due diligence exercise contemplated by
the Letter of Intent and would have unilaterally reset the terms of the Letter
of Intent.

[
44
]

In doing so, Mr. Potten would have breached
his obligation to act in good faith towards the conclusion of the contemplated
deal, contrary to his obligations under the
Civil Code of Quebec
.
[13]
He would also have failed to honour his obligations, as per the
Letter of Intent, to do everything necessary to permit Mr. Ryer to carry
out the due diligence necessary for the transaction to close.
[14]

2.2

Mr. Potten and the Company

[
45
]

Mr. Potten states that he fully cooperated with the due
diligence process, within his means and within what was reasonably
available.

[
46
]

He claims
that the deal did not go through because of the business disagreement which
arose concerning the allocation of the Company’s 2011 fiscal year profits.  This
disagreement, and the parties’ inability to resolve it, would not in any manner
be attributable to his alleged bad faith.

[
47
]

Mr. Potten
also pleads that Mr. Ryer was to be 50-50 partner with Mr. Greendpoon
in the acquisition.  At most, Mr. Ryer would therefore be entitled to 50%
of the damages sustained and of the profits lost.  He could not claim
Mr. Greenspoon’s share in same.

[
48
]

Finally, Mr. Potten argues that Mr. Ryer abused his
rights in the context of the present business and legal dispute, and should
therefore pay for all damages sustained as a result.

3.

THE ISSUES IN DISPUTE

[
49
]

Hence, the issues in dispute present as follows:

THE
PRINCIPLE CLAIM OF MR. RYER

1.         Have Mr. Potten or the Company breached their
obligation to negotiate and cooperate in good faith towards the conclusion of
an agreement respecting the terms of the Letter of Intent?

2.         What damages resulted from such a breach, in any?

3.         Can Mr. Ryer claim Mr. Greenspoon’s share in
the alleged damages and losses?

THE CROSS-CLAIM OF MR. POTTEN

4.         Is Mr. Ryer’s claim abusive or has he otherwise
triggered his extracontractual liability towards Mr. Potten, in the
context of their business and legal dispute?

4.

THE ANALYSIS

THE
PRINCIPLE CLAIM OF MR. RYER

4.1

Did the Defendants breach their obligation to
negotiate and cooperate in good faith towards the conclusion of an agreement respecting
the terms of the Letter of Intent?

[
50
]

Mr. Ryer claims that the Defendants did not
act in good faith both in the due diligence process and in unilaterally
resetting the agreement of the parties concerning the ownership of the
Company’s 2011 profits.

[
51
]

The Court does not share Mr. Ryer’s views.

[
52
]

The Defendants acted in good faith throughout.

[
53
]

The deal did not materialize as a result of a
legitimate disagreement which arose between the parties on a major issue: the
ownership of the 2011 profits.  The negative outcome is in no way attributable
to any of the parties’ bad faith in the conduct of the due diligence or of the
negotiations.

4.1.1

The good faith in the conduct of the due diligence

[
54
]

With respect to the due diligence, Mr. Ryer
decries that:

54.1.

they were never given the opportunity to speak
to suppliers, employees or customers;

54.2.

many of the standard financial reports and much
of the information requested were not communicated; and

54.3.

they were only given access to the premises of
the Company after business hours.

[
55
]

The Court, however, holds that throughout the
discussions, Mr. Potten made the necessary efforts to ensure that the
buyers be provided with the documentation and information needed for the
transaction.  He cooperated in good faith with the due diligence.

[
56
]

For instance, very early in the process,
Mr. Potten has put the buyers in contact with those persons who possessed
the knowledge required to respond to their questions and information requests.
To that effect, he gave them full access to his business consultant
(Mr. Mazoff), to the Company’s bankers (Mr. Ciolfi, TD Bank), and to
the Company’s external auditors (Mr. Corber, RSM Richter).  He instructed
them to provide all necessary information to the potential buyers.

[
57
]

Mr. Potten also attended six meetings with
the buyers,
[15]
organized a meeting with the company’s bankers
[16]
, and attended two meetings with Roynat.  During all those meetings,
Mr. Potten remained fully cooperative and participative.
[17]

[
58
]

Throughout the discussions, the buyers were
specifically provided with the following financial information, at their
request:

58.1.

Financial statements of the Company and
normalized EBITDAs for the years 2006, 2007, 2008 and 2009;
[18]

58.2.

Memorandum describing the business, the
market/competition, the threats/opportunities and of the shipments over the
years;
[19]

58.3.

2010 audited financial statements;
[20]

58.4.

Schedule of normalized earnings from 1992 to
2010;
[21]

58.5.

Company’s banking Agreement with the TD Bank;
[22]

58.6.

Company’s historical financial information,
provided by the external auditors of the Company;
[23]
and

58.7.

Inventory statements, Ceridian’s Report on
Controls places in Operation and Tests of Operating effectiveness (2008-2009),
lease, etc.
[24]

[
59
]

Even if on occasion, some of the information had
to be reviewed with the Company to ensure its accuracy, the buyers nevertheless
expressed that it was sufficiently helpful to meet their needs.
[25]
They obtained the necessary cooperation from the Company to update
the information, when necessary.

[
60
]

Mr. Potten even acceded to Mr. Ryer’s
request and authorized the external auditors of the Company to adjust the 2011
forecasts which the buyers intended to use to obtain financing, along Mr. Ryer’s
suggestions and recommendations.
[26]

[
61
]

Some discussions eventually occurred on the
difficulty and necessity for the potential buyers to access more extensive
information.  However, no serious issue arose in this regard.

[
62
]

For instance, on January 11, 2010, Mr. Ryer
provided Mr. Mazoff with a check list for the due diligence (
Due
diligence check list
).
[27]
Mr. Ryer prepared this list from the template which Fraser
Milner Casgrain (
FMC
), the buyer’s legal advisors to the transaction,
had provided to him a month earlier, on or about December 16, 2010.

[
63
]

The Due diligence check list was discussed on January
12, 2010 at a meeting with Messrs Potten, Ryer, Greenspoon, Mazoff and
Roynat representative, Mr. Éric Krause.  After this discussion, it was narrowed
down to almost half of the requests.

[
64
]

On February 9, 2011, at the initiative of
Mr. Ryer, a further meeting took place at the offices of the Company, with
the view to moving the due diligence process forward.  Messrs Ryer,
Greenspoon, Mazoff, Potten and two Roynat representatives (Messrs André
Laforge and Eric Krause) attended the meeting.

[
65
]

Another revised due diligence check list was
sent to Mr. Mazoff on the following day and Roynat provided a list of the
important outstanding information from their perspective.
[28]

[
66
]

Admittedly, after the meeting of February 9,
2011, access to the due diligence material requested
was not as easy and extensive as Mr. Ryer would have preferred.
Nevertheless, these difficulties did not amount to obstruction or a bad faith
attempt by Mr. Potten to abort the transaction or discourage the buyers.

[
67
]

Even if some items were outstanding and required
further investigation with the seller,
[29]
the tone still remained very positive between the parties.

[
68
]

For instance, Roynat, who insisted on a proper
due diligence review before irrevocably committing to financing the
transaction, did not see any major obstacle in this regard.  In an email dated
January 27, 2011, Roynat stated:

From your comments we can see
that many usual reports found in businesses are not available
. This could be expected from a simple man running a simple
business.

I would not worry too much and
will check with Andre if there are reports we absolutely need. I am sure we can
answer most questions when we all sit down together again
.
[30]

[Emphasis added]

[
69
]

Access to the clients and to the suppliers also became an issue at
one point.  Mr. Ryer felt that he should be given such access.  Mr. Potten,
on the other hand, rather felt that the buyers should only access such
priceless information and contacts after providing an executed definitive offer
to finance the acquisition.

[
70
]

Such an
executed definitive offer never came.  The parties ended up disagreeing on
another aspect (ownership of 2011 profits) before the issues of access to
suppliers, clients and the premises of the Company during business hours became
serious.

[
71
]

Mr. Ryer is now overstating the
difficulties encountered in conducting the due diligence.

[
72
]

Actually, Mr. Ryer received enough
information to secure serious financing offers from two lenders to finance the
transaction (Roynat
[31]
and
Desjardins
[32]
).

[
73
]

Interestingly, he also represented, in an email
of February 16, 2011 to Desjardins, a potential lender, that he was satisfied
with the manner in which the due diligence was progressing:

The Due diligence is progressing
well with no surprises to date
. Steve will be
providing an analysis of the annual sales, by customer, to us before end of
week and we will forward same to you immediately thereafter.
[33]

[Emphasis added]

4.1.2

The good faith in addressing the matter of
ownership of the 2011 profits

[
74
]

The negotiations did not come to a fruitful
outcome as a result of the disagreement of the parties on a crucial issue: the
ownership of the profits earned and received during the negotiation of the transaction.
This disagreement was material.  The parties were unable to resolve it.

[
75
]

Mr. Ryer claims that the parties had
previously discussed this issue and had agreed in this regard.  He blames
Mr. Potten for unilaterally, in bad faith, resetting the terms of the
Letter of Intent on the issue of ownership of the 2011 profits.

[
76
]

As more fully explained below, the Court does
not share Mr. Ryer’s views in this regard for two reasons: (1) the Letter
of Intent did not unequivocally address the issue; and (2) the parties made the
necessary and good-faith efforts to overcome this major hurdle, albeit without
success.

4.1.2.1

The terms of the Letter of Intent on the
ownership of the profits earned and received before the closing

[
77
]

The parties obviously did not clearly and
unequivocally address this issue in the Letter of Intent.

[
78
]

The Letter of Intent sets the purchase price at $11.75
million.
[34]

[
79
]

It also includes a Net Book Value clause (
NBV
Clause
), which reads as follows:

4.5.

The balance sheet of the Target [(Company)] as at Closing [(February 22, 2011)]
shall reflect a
minimum
Net Book Value (as defined under GAAP and
calculated
in a manner consistent with past practice of the Target) of

$7.7 million
.
[35]

[Emphasis added]

[
80
]

Admittedly, the NBV Clause is of some relevance
to the issue of sharing the profits earned before the closing date.

[
81
]

However, Messrs Potten, Ryer and Greenspoon
together have three different readings of what the Letter of Intent provided on
the ownership of the profits earned during the negotiation period.  Their
respective versions significantly differ as to what the requirement of a
minimum $7.7 million NBV at closing permitted or precluded Mr. Potten from
doing with those profits.

[
82
]

According to Mr. Potten, the profits earned
before the February 22, 2011 closing date could be remitted to him in the form
of dividends, bonus or otherwise, as long as the NBV of the Company at closing
was not below $7.7 million.  Over the preceding years, he had always taken his
share of the profits out of the Company through the payment of bonuses and
dividends.
[36]
The more the busy season was underway and the more the 2011 year
“was in the books” at the time of closing, the more Mr. Potten felt
entitled to the 2011 profits.  Mr. Potten’s understanding would therefore
be consistent with the Company’s past practice, as the NBV Clause provides.

[
83
]

Mr. Ryers has a different view, which
respectfully may, in some respects, appear somewhat incoherent.

[
84
]

To a certain extent, Mr. Ryer shares
Mr. Potten’s view that the issue of profit split was indirectly addressed
through the NBV Clause.  Mr. Ryer actually testifies that the Letter of
Intent did not have to deal with the issue of profit splitting, as the NBV
Clause protected that.

[
85
]

On the one hand, Mr. Ryer sees the NBV
Clause as a snap-shot clause which only comes into play at closing, at which
time the NBV must be equal to or above $7.7 million.  As long as the NBV
at closing was $7.7 million or more, this provision would accordingly not
prevent Mr. Potten from withdrawing a dividend or bonus of a non material
magnitude (up to $200,000) prior to closing.  According to Mr. Ryer’s
understanding, the payment of a greater dividend or bonus to Mr. Potten
prior to the closing would amount to a breach of the NBV Clause, even if the
NBV at closing remained at $7.7 million or more.

[
86
]

On the other hand, Mr. Ryer admits that:

86.1.

a purchase of all shares of the Company was
contemplated.  Hence, everything made it clear, from his perspective, that the
profits belonged to the Company, and that the buyers would control the
Company.  He nevertheless concedes that the change of control was to occur only
at the date of closing.

86.2.

Whatever profits were in fiscal year 2011, as
long as the NBV was $7.7 million at closing, the rest could go to
Mr. Potten;

86.3.

If the projections
[37]

materialized, the amount which Mr. Potten would be allowed to take out
would be greater as the year goes on;

86.4.

Prior to closing, the purchasers exercise no
influence on the Company.  Mr. Potten could therefore keep the profits
from the sales made prior to the closing date.

[
87
]

Mr. Greenspoon exposes a third, and much
more rigid, understanding of the NBV Clause.

[
88
]

Mr. Greenspoon initially suggested that the
payment of the dividends or bonuses before closing was permitted, as long as
the banking covenants of the Company were respected.

[
89
]

He later indicated in his testimony that the NBV
Clause provides for
minimum
NBV such that any NBV above this minimum
would belong to the buyer.  Hence, the terms of the Letter of Intent would have
prevented Mr. Potten from receiving any dividend or bonus, prior to
closing, even as low as $100,000, and even if the NBV remained at $7.7 million
or exceeded that amount at closing.

[
90
]

With such conflicting views, the Court cannot
hold that the Letter of Intent clearly provided that the 2011 profits belonged
to the buyers and that Mr. Potten was unilaterally, and in bad faith,
trying to reset the terms of the Letter of Intent when he insisted on keeping
such profits.

4.1.2.2

The Parties’ good faith attempts to solve their
disagreement on this material issue

[
91
]

The parties attempted in good faith to resolve
this major disagreement, which arose in the course of the negotiations.

[
92
]

Mr. Potten has been open and upfront.
Through Mr. Mazoff, he gave an advance warning that the issue could arise,
particularly if the closing was eventually postponed.  As early as October 26,
2010, bearing the Company’s seasonal business cycle in mind, he emphasized the
importance of closing the transaction before the calendar year end:

We need to aim for a deal by the
end of the year for many reasons as already discussed
. One additional compelling reason is that
if a deal happens once
the season is well underway or almost done, Steve is going to want to keep a
big share of the year profits
.
[38]

[Emphasis added]

[
93
]

Mr. Potten has openly put his cards on the
table.  He promptly, prudently and diligently raised the issue before going
further with the negotiations.
[39]

[
94
]

Mr. Potten eventually cancelled the
February 17, 2011 meeting a few hours before the scheduled time.  Mr. Potten
informed Mr. Ryer that it was a very busy period, that he had not had the
chance of gathering the additional materials requested and that he would
therefore not be able to respect the meeting plan.

[
95
]

Mr. Ryer claims that Mr. Mazoff would
have called him shortly after and indicated that “ the deal was
dead ”, as the Company’s performances in February were better than
expected, and as Mr. Potten did not want to relinquish the profits of
2011.

[
96
]

Mr. Ryer’s email to Roynat on the following
day however does not reflect that alarming picture. It only states that the
meeting had to be postponed as Mr. Potten had not been able to prepare the
requested information, due to the busy season.
[40]

[
97
]

Still, Mr. Ryer approached Mr. Mazoff shortly
thereafter to request an extension of the Letter of Intent and of the due
diligence delay.
[41]

[
98
]

Mr. Potten’s attorney, Mtre Cohen, then
clearly indicated to the buyers that an agreement on the ownership of the 2011
profits was a prerequisite to an agreement on a postponement of the closing
date:

[Mr. Potten] would like the
[extension] letter to indicate that
the purpose of the meeting is to address
the issue of who gets the profit for the year ending June 30, 2011, given that
the time frame for closing will be different from that originally contemplated
in the LOI.  As I understand it, the reality is that this issue will need to be
addressed and resolved (From both sides perspective) if there is to be a
transaction
.

Am I wasting my time if I try to
come up with the wording to put in the extension letter concerning same?
[42]

[Emphasis added]

[
99
]

Mr. Ryer replied that he was hopeful that
the parties could overcome this hurdle and that pursuing the discussions would
not be a waste of time :

I don’t believe you are wasting
your time as I remain hopeful that we can bring this transaction to fruition
- we must have an understanding of the new deal being proposed by
the vendor in order to move forward.
[43]

[Emphasis added]

[
100
]

On March 8, 2011, during another meeting organized by
Mr. Potten, the latter exposed the highlights of new terms he proposed for
the deal, which he felt appropriately addressed the issue of ownership of the
2011 profits:
[44]

•

Reduction of the purchase price by $500,000
(from $11.75 million to $11.25 million);

•

Increase of the Company’s Net Book Value (
NBV
)
at closing by $200,000  (from $7.7 million to $7.9 million);

•

2011 profits to remain with Mr. Potten ($2.5
million to $3 million);

•

Two-phase due diligence period: Phase I: until
March 15, 2011.  Phase II: from June 2, 2011 to closing.

[
101
]

Messrs Ryer and Greenspoon were extremely dissatisfied with these
new proposed terms and walked away.   The meeting lasted less than 30 minutes.

[
102
]

In Messrs Ryer and Greenspoon’s view, Mr. Potten keeping
profits of more than $2 million entirely changed the economics of the
deal.  From their perspective, the proposed adjustments fell short of restoring
the economic balance originally contemplated in the Letter of Intent.

[
103
]

More particularly, lowering the purchase price by $500,000 was
clearly not sufficient.  Increasing the NBV by $2 million also made no
difference from their perspective.  To them, it was just the equivalent of a
reassurance to the effect that the Company would not sell any major asset and
would not change its complexion.

[
104
]

Even though Mr. Greenspoon concedes that many items of the
revised deal terms
[45]
are not objectionable, he maintains that he and Mr. Ryer were
not interested in this new proposed transaction and decided not to negotiate
it. “That deal was dead on delivery”, he says.  They would not pay $11.25
million for a business where $3 million of profits would remain with the
vendor.

[
105
]

Later in the afternoon of March 8, 2011, within hours of the abrupt
termination of the meeting, Mr. Potten called Mr. Greenspoon to
welcome any counterproposal to the revised terms he had presented.

[
106
]

On the next day, they met for lunch.  Mr. Potten enquired if
there was still a way to make the transaction happen.

[
107
]

Discussions between Mr. Greenspoon and Mtre Cohen,
Mr. Potten’s attorney, followed.  In Mid-April 2014, Mr. Greenspoon
claims that he sent him what he felt correctly reflected their discussions on
the terms of a proposed new Letter of Intent, with a revised purchase price of $9
million.

[
108
]

Mtre Cohen allegedly told Mr. Greenspoon that he was confident
that Mr. Potten would sign the new Letter of Intent, upon returning from
his trip to China.  Mr. Greenspoon claims that he never heard back from
him.

[
109
]

This new Letter of Intent is not filed.  This important factual
element is also not alluded to in the Motion to institute proceedings or in its
two subsequent amended versions.  Roynat was also not made aware of the
proposed revised deal terms which Mr. Potten presented on March 8, 2011. There
is also no evidence or suggestion that Roynat was informed in a new proposed
acquisition price at $9 million.

[
110
]

The Court is of the view that both the evidence and the allegations
in Plaintiff’s proceedings show that notwithstanding Mr. Potten’s
invitation to make a counter offer, no serious or official counter offer was
made to Mr. Potten and the Company after Mr. Ryer and Mr. Greenspoon
waked away from the March 8, 2011 meeting.

[
111
]

It is a well known principle that the right to disagree and to
refuse to enter into a contract is part of the contractual freedom of the
parties.  The obligation to negotiate in good faith and collaborate towards the
conclusion of a contract does not amount to an absolute obligation to
ultimately agree.  If a material disagreement arises, a party can terminate the
negotiations, provided that such termination is done in a reasonable manner,
not abusively.
[46]

[
112
]

In the case at hand, the parties faced an obstacle which they were
unable to overcome, in spite of their reasonable and good faith efforts.

[
113
]

The impact of a postponement of the closing date on certain terms of
a deal is not unique to the present case.  Delaying a transaction may indeed
impact on the economics of an acquisition.  Understandably, such postponement
may require adjustments to the purchase price or other parameters of the deal, taking
into account the profits made by the continuing operations until closing.
[47]

[
114
]

By the end of February, it became clear to all, including
Mr. Ryer, that the 2011 fiscal year was in the
books and that the revenues booked in January and February had exceeded
forecasts.
[48]
Hence, it was reasonable (if not obvious) that a debate over the
ownership of these profits would arise, even more acutely if the closing date
was to be postponed.

[
115
]

The outcome of the present case does not lie with who the Court
considers was right.  Suffice to say that although conflicting, each party’s
views on the ownership of the 2011 profits were legitimate and reasonable.
Each party thus had the right to end the negotiations and walk away. Before
walking away, the parties made good faith attempts to overcome that hurdle,
without success.

[
116
]

Clearly, the negotiations ended with a high level of frustration,
but without any bad faith from any of the parties.

4.2

What damages resulted from such a breach, if
any?

[
117
]

The Court had the benefit of hearing and weighing the evidence
tendered on damages.  Even though, as explained above, Mr. Ryer’s action
is dismissed, some comments on the damages claimed are in order.

[
118
]

Mr. Ryer’s claim for damages has varied as follows over the
course of his law suit:

May
20, 2011

Motion
to Institute Proceedings

May
22, 2012

Amended
Motion to Institute Proceedings

20, 2014

Re
–Amended Motion to Institute Proceedings

4.2.1

The loss of profits ($3,514,647.00)

[
119
]

The claim for loss of profits is based on the normalized pre-tax
profits which the Company earned for 2011 and 2012.
[49]

[
120
]

It includes a claim for the benefit of unreported cash sales.  The
reference to unreported cash sales was added on the second day of trial.  This
late addition appears to have been made mostly in an attempt to embarrass
Mr. Potten.  The same remark applies to Mr. Ryer’s testimony at trial
on the elements in the financial statements of the Company which may have been
suggestive of fraud, namely: fluctuating gross margins, inventories and sales.

[
121
]

Mr. Ryer justifiably takes pride in his fraud examiner
certification.  Especially in view of such credentials, the fact that he raises
theses irregularities for the first time at trial and then amends his claim to
seek the benefit of alleged unreported cash sales which he expected to keep,
and inevitably conceal too, is questionable, to say the least.

[
122
]

Also, Mr. Ryer’s claim for loss of profits overlooks the fact
that he and Mr. Greenspoon would have had to pay a
purchase price of between $11.75 million and $9 million to receive any part of the Company’s profit.  Mr. Ryer’s claim
does not account for said purchase price.

4.2.2

Consulting Fees ($46,870.84)

[
123
]

This claim is made for the legal fees which the purchasers incurred
in pursuing the acquisition.

[
124
]

In this regard, the Court highlights the following key points:

124.1.

In the Letter of Intent,
[50]
the
parties agreed that the parties would each bear their own costs in respect of
the transaction;

124.2.

Some of the professional fees relating to
Fraser, Milner, Casgrain remain unpaid;
[51]

124.3.

Some of the fees relating to both RSM Richter
and FMC were incurred for the renegotiations in March 2011, which were optional
for the purchasers to incur and which they did at the risk of not being able to
come to new terms; and

124.4.

None of these expenses are addressed to
Mr. Ryer personnally.  All the bills are made to a holding company, which
is not a party to the present claim.

4.2.3

Loss of time/inconvenience ($125,000.00)

[
125
]

Mr. Ryer bases this claim on an estimation of the 400 hours
which he lost working on the transaction, at his tax consultant hourly rate
($200-$500).

[
126
]

However, the evidence shows that at the relevant time, Mr. Ryer
was employed by Milos Restaurant, where he earned an annual base salary of
$200,000.
[52]
He states that he left this position in November 2010 to pursue
the transaction. At the same time, Mr. Ryer testifies that there were no
serious discussions after the March 8, 2011 meeting, where Mr. Potten
proposed revised terms.  Accordingly, his claim would only relate to a period
of four months (December, January, February and March).

[
127
]

Mr. Ryer’s $200,000 claim for loss of time and inconvenience
falls on the high side, as the evidence shows that he would likely have earned
approximately $67,000 over that four-month period.
[53]

[
128
]

Mr. Ryer also offered no convincing evidence to the effect that
he was prevented from generating similar revenues after March 2011, as a result
of the time he invested working towards the conclusion of a deal for the
acquisition of the Company.

4.3

Can Mr. Ryer claim Mr. Greenspoon’s
share in the alleged damages and losses?

[
129
]

Mr. Greenspoon is not party to the action.  He explains that at
the time of execution of the Letter of Intent, he was in the course of
negotiating severance with his employer.  Signing the Letter of Intent would
therefore have put him at a strategic disadvantage in this severance
negotiation with his former employer.  Mr. Greenspoon therefore decided
not to sign the Letter of Intent.

[
130
]

Mr. Greenspoon and Mr. Ryer nevertheless agreed that they
were to be equal partners in the transaction.  More particularly, Mr. Ryer and Mr. Greenspoon were to be 50% partners of the
holding company to be formed for the acquisition of the Company.  It has always
been clear that Mr. Greenspoon and Mr. Ryer would equally share the
costs and benefits of this business adventure.

[
131
]

Mr. Ryer is claiming Mr. Greenspoon’s share in the alleged
loss benefits of the transaction, notwithstanding the fact that
Mr. Greenspoon is not a party to the present action.

[
132
]

Mr. Ryer cannot make such a claim on behalf of
Mr. Greenspoon.  The latter, for his own reasons, decided not to make any
claim.  He has to bear the consequences of his choice.

[
133
]

In addition, the holding company which was to be formed for the acquisition
of the Company has never been incorporated and is not a party to the present
action.  This situation is very different from the one in
Pegasus Partners Inc.
v.
Groupe
Laurem inc.
,
[54]
a precedent which Mr. Ryer erroneously invokes to his benefit.

THE
CROSS-CLAIM OF MR. POTTEN

4.4

Is Mr. Ryer’s claim abusive or has he
otherwise triggered his extracontractual liability towards Mr. Potten, in
the context of their business and legal dispute?

[
134
]

As Cross-Plaintiff, Mr. Potten claims $350,000 from Mr. Ryer
for moral and punitive damages resulting from his abusive lawsuit and conduct.

[
135
]

Mr. Ryer’s case against the Defendants was certainly not as
strong as the latter’ defence.  Nevertheless, Mr. Ryer’s claim against
Mr. Potten and the Company is not in itself ill founded to a point
amounting to an abuse of right.  To paraphrase the Court of Appeal in
Acadia
Subaru
, the Court does not conclude here that Mr. Ryer has brought the
present suit, although unfounded, “in a manner that is so patent, or so
frivolous or dilatory as to be an abuse of process”.
[55]

[
136
]

Still, Mr. Potten also bases his cross-claim on another ground:
a series of e-mails which Mr. Ryer personally sent to him from March to
June, 2012, in the course of the present proceedings, with the apparent view of
annoying him.  These emails to Mr. Potten, include:

136.1.

a copy of a SténoFac invoice for the deposition
of Mr. Potten (March 13, 2012, 4:10 p.m.);

136.2.

a letter to Mr. Potten’s attorney
concerning the communication of undertakings and the threat of bringing a
motion to dismiss Mr. Potten’s plea and for pecuniary sanctions (April 16,
2012, 9:49 p.m.);

136.3.

an invitation to a golf tournament (May 28,
2012, 3:40 p.m.);

136.4.

an e-mail asking Mr. Potten why his ending
inventory was so low and that he would be communicating with his accountants to
inquire (June 1, 2012, 12:53 p.m.);

136.5.

an article by Me David Stolow and Me James
Bunting of Davies, his lawfirm, entitled “walking away from the table:
pre-contractual documents and duty to negotiate in good faith” (June 22, 2012).
[56]

[
137
]

On June 22, 2012, Mr. Potten amended his plea to address this issue
and claims damages for what he felt was harassing and intimidating.
[57]

[
138
]

Thereafter, Mr. Ryer included Mr. Potten to his list of e-mail
contacts and sent him a series of additional e-mails.

[
139
]

These e-mails include:

139.1.

a link to “Men’s Health Summary – Fall Guide to
Style – By Robin Behar – Click Here” (October 18, 2012, 2:37 p.m.);

139.2.

an article entitled “AMRN/3Q12 Recap: Awaiting
NCE Determination and Potential Business Development/Outperform” (November 9, 2012,
2:20 p.m.);

139.3.

a donation request for the Starlight children’s
foundation ( December 10, 2012 p.m.);

139.4.

an invitation to participate at the Rumble at
the Ritz event (February 19, 2013);

139.5.

a series of pictures depicting World War II
events and Holocaust survivors (July 30, 2013, 10:19 a.m.);

139.6.

Jewish New Year wishes (September 3, 2013 12:34
p.m.);

139.7.

an article entitled “is your manliness losing
its swagger?” (October 25, 2013, 4:13 p.m.);

139.8.

an invitation to an art exhibition featuring
Heidi Spector (February 4, 2014, 11:48 a.m.); and

139.9.

a link to an article from the
Globe and Mail

entitled “Law firm Heenan Blaikie wobbles as more lawyers leave”.

[
140
]

Mr. Ryer never shared such information and solicitations with Mr. Potten
before the Fall of 2012.

[
141
]

On April 26, 2013, after being apprised that Mr. Potten was in
negotiations with another potential purchaser, Mr. Ryer also sent a demand
letter to Mr. Potten by e-mail, putting him on notice that he would take necessary
actions if such a sale should take place.
[58]

[
142
]

The Court holds that Mr. Ryer did not innocently send all these
communications to Mr. Potten.  These continuing communications by
Mr. Ryer to Mr. Potten amounted to harassment and intimidation.
Mr. Ryer acted in a grossly inappropriate manner in repeatedly
communicating with Mr. Potten as he did, pending the outcome of the
current litigation.  Such a conduct is incompatible with Mr. Ryer’s alleged
stature.

[
143
]

However, there is no sufficient proof that this harassing and
immature behaviour on the part of Mr. Ryer resulted directly in damages to
Mr. Potten.

[
144
]

The evidence which Mr. Potten submitted on the extent of his
damages and their actual cause is indeed minimal.  Mr. Potten states that
he sustained stress and anxiety as a result of Mr. Ryer’s harassment.  He
testifies that he has difficulty sleeping, lost his zest for life and cannot
work normally.  The evidence does not enable the Court to attribute such
damages to Mr. Ryer’s fault, as opposed to the unfavourable outcome of the
negotiations or to the existence of the current litigation.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
145
]

DISMISSES
the Mr. Lennie Ryer’s
claim
WITH COSTS
;

[
146
]

DISMISSES
the Cross-Claim of
Mr. Steve Potten
WITH COSTS
